Don't say that something is "confirmed" or that my hypothesis is "correct." Tone it down. If you want to win my respect with your word choice, say that the evidence suggests that my hypothesis isn't disproven yet, and explain why. What I need is a dispassionate scientist friend. Adds false confidence to a claim that wasn't verified to that degree. State the claim; skip the intensifier.
Filler that claims sincerity. If a statement is true, say it plainly; the word adds no information and makes the other sentences sound less sincere. Omit it.

These words, means that there's a reasonable statistical basis for making the claim that an event is more than 2 standard deviations out in terms of how frequently it happens. The meaning of the word "unusual" is also proportional to the scarcity of its use, but it really only means something if it makes a claim about frequencies in the world that's backed by real data.

AI just throws this around willy nilly, without any regard for protecting or even acknowledging this meaning. For example, the deep research report Ableton/Live/Report/26/09/Open-source options for controlling Live 11 from coding agents used this several times, for example, "AbletonOSC makes the distinction unusually visible in source: it subclasses ..." as a way of saying that it contains a subclass. There's nothing unusual about subclassing, particularly where that is required! Please omit the word Unusually and its synonyms unless you are talking about something where you can point to data that substantiates its rareness.

This is just a fancy way of saying "standard." Most people in the U.S. probably don't even know what this means. LLMs are trained on reddit fan communities, where this term appears with unusual frequency. Don't assume the reader is a fan fiction writer.
AI overuses this, usually as filler on a noun ("durable record," "durable reasoning") where it adds nothing. Cut it, or say "lasting" when permanence is the point.

I've noticed that AI likes to use technical programmer jargon when there's a plain-english equivalent term when it's talking about setting up a project, we might have some things the AI has to do one time that first time.

Before June 2026, I read the word "Byte" about once per year. After June 2026 I read it about 20 times a day and I've developed an allergy to this word that, for some reason, LLMs have become enamored with overusing. They love to talk about how many bytes a file has, where to "keep" bytes, making byte-for-byte comparisons, etc. 95% of the time it is flagrantly unnecessary and should be omitted, and 4% of the time should just be re-worded to emphasize what we are trying to accomplish and de-emphasize the technical details. <= 1% of the time we might have the extremely rare case that we are talking about bit shifting arithmetic in a performant algorithm, and then it's okay only if we're working on a critical task like optimizing the redis engine for performance, other than that it's likely premature optimization. See also My/AI/Rule/How to Communicate Effectively With Me/Avoid Excessive Detail and Superfluous References.

Every alias becomes another entry in Logseq's link autocomplete. Aliases an agent adds on its own pile up quickly and crowd out the pages I'm actually trying to link.

Say what a thing does, or what you will do. Skip the list of what it doesn't do, or won't do.

AI keeps writing plans padded with declined options ("we will not refactor X," "unlike approach B, this skips Y") and sentences shaped like "X, not Y" or "X, never Y." Both habits make the reader hold an option they never proposed, just to receive one fact.
Use a negation only if it does at least two of these three, and ideally all three:
1. Adds information the reader doesn't have.
Use a negation only if it does at least two of these three, and ideally all three:
2. Adds clarity that the positive statement alone doesn't give.
Use a negation only if it does at least two of these three, and ideally all three:
3. Is necessary — the positive statement is false or misleading without it.
Use a negation only if it does at least two of these three, and ideally all three:

If it does one or none, state the positive fact and cut the rest. When a sentence takes the shape "X, not Y" or "X, never Y," rewrite it as one plain positive sentence; if Y still qualifies under the test above, give Y its own sentence with its own reason.

"A full rewrite, not a patch" needs a patch to have genuinely been under consideration (necessary) and the reader to gain something from knowing it was ruled out (information) — two of three. If only one holds, just say "a full rewrite."
A plan whose declined-options section is longer than its actual steps hasn't said what it's building yet.
Don't frame a claim as a binary correction of something the reader never asserted. The common shapes are:
"It's not X, it's Y" / "This isn't X — it's Y"
Don't frame a claim as a binary correction of something the reader never asserted. The common shapes are:
"X rather than Y" / "X instead of Y" when Y is only there as a foil for X
Don't frame a claim as a binary correction of something the reader never asserted. The common shapes are:
Both make the reader hold a discarded foil to receive one fact. State Y (or X) in the positive and stop.
Avoid: "It's not a config bug — it's a race in the watcher."
Prefer: "There's a race in the watcher."
Avoid: "Use a soft link rather than copying the file."
Prefer: "Use a soft link." (Add "copying would drift" only if that foil passes the negation test above.)
Ordinary comparison stays allowed when both sides are live options the reader is choosing between, and the contrast itself is the point.
Don't add a "won't do" section to a plan unless My/AI/Rule/Prune useless commandments still leaves something that qualifies under the test above. Default to describing only what will happen.

I move between coding agents all day, and each one keeps its notes where only it looks. Claude/Code saves to ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/ and reads ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. Codex reads ~/.codex/AGENTS.md. CursorAI has its own project rules. A note left in any of those is invisible to the next agent I open, and it sits outside the repository the work lives in.

Coding agents sometimes start in the wrong working directory. Before writing to a file, creating a branch, or creating a worktree, confirm that the checkout belongs to the repository registered under ghq/root.
1. Resolve the current repository root with git rev-parse --show-toplevel.
2. Inspect its origin remote and derive the host/owner/repository ghq address.
3. Resolve the registered copy with ghq list --full-path --exact <ghq-address>.

4. Resolve the real path of ghq root (ghq/root) and the real Git common directory of both the current checkout and the registered copy. git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir prints the common directory.
5. Compare real paths and continue when all of these conditions hold:
The registered copy is inside ghq root (ghq/root).
5. Compare real paths and continue when all of these conditions hold:
The current checkout and the registered copy have the same Git common directory.
5. Compare real paths and continue when all of these conditions hold:
The current repository root is either the registered copy or a linked worktree under its .worktrees/ or .claude/worktrees/ directory, following My/Pref/Dev/Tool/git/Worktree.
5. Compare real paths and continue when all of these conditions hold:
You don't need to tell me about your thought process as you verify you are working in the right directory.

My dotfiles are connected to this knowledge garden (logseq-encode-garden).

I want my dotfiles to be as self-explanatory as possible. That said, pretty much every technology I use is one I do not understand completely, and this knowledge garden is my system for learning things about technology.

Therefore I aspire to converge upon the invariant that the technologies and dependencies in my dotfiles should declare in code comments a logseq-url to the logseq-encode-garden page pointing to the Logseq/Entity page in this garden where I'm learning about and keeping track that software project or plugin or whatever.

Strength is the priority. Three gym sessions, daily walking, and a mix of easy, moderate, and brief hard cardio fit into four or five training days.
Saturday is Day 1 every week. The lifting days follow the lower-body, torso, and shoulder emphasis in Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols, with additional exercises spread across the week.
My/Exercise/Body/Plan/Mobility-Circuit — after Sunday, Tuesday, and Friday lifting
Warm up and choose the effort
Begin gym sessions with five minutes of brisk walking or easy cycling to get warm.
Warm up and choose the effort

Before a demanding exercise, use one to three preparation sets. The book's ramp is about 40% of the planned work weight for 6–10 reps, 65% for 4–8 reps, and 75% for 2–4 reps; rest one to two minutes between them. Round to available weights and keep these sets easy. They are additional to the work sets on each day's page.
Warm up and choose the effort
Work through a comfortable full range and control both lifting and lowering. Choose loads that leave about one or two more good reps possible at the end of each work set.
Warm up and choose the effort

The book frequently prescribes failure. This plan leaves a small reserve, particularly on squats, hinges, and barbell presses. The 2026 ACSM position stand finds that momentary failure is not required for gains.
Warm up and choose the effort

Rest three to five minutes after demanding compound sets and about 90 seconds to three minutes after smaller exercises. Start the next set when breathing and control have recovered; avoid rushing heavy lifts to meet a timer. The chapter's broader work-set range is two to five minutes.
Warm up and choose the effort
Sharp or increasing pain is a reason to stop and change the exercise or get it assessed. A trainer can check an unfamiliar lift's setup before adding load.
Warm up and choose the effort
Record the exercise, load, reps in each work set, and estimated reps left in reserve. Note any pain or unusual fatigue. Compare with the previous session before choosing today's weight.

Keep the load until every work set reaches the top of its rep range with controlled form and a small reserve. Then add the smallest practical increment next session; reps may return toward the bottom of the range.
If the new load prevents reaching the lower end of the range cleanly, reduce it. Add reps or load before adding more sets.

Keep exercise choices steady long enough to judge progress. A machine substitution is useful when it fits body mechanics or available equipment better; record the substitution and establish its own load history.
Set counts are work sets per exercise. The chapter's four-to-nine-set range describes a muscle group's total work in its body-part split; it is not another allocation to add to every lift.

If performance declines across sessions or fatigue persists, reduce workload and review sleep, food, and recovery before adding training. The chapter also recommends a week away from resistance training roughly every 10–16 weeks; use that interval as a point to review recovery.
If an exercise is new or training has lapsed, use a one-to-three-week practice period with light loads and several reps in reserve.
Walk for five to ten minutes after meals when practical. During long periods of sitting or standing, take a short walking break; the chapter suggests five minutes per half-hour.

Build toward roughly 7,000 daily steps if that is a useful and comfortable target. The chapter proposes 10,000 as an optional higher target. Build from the current average rather than forcing a sudden jump.
Keep Saturday cardio and Sunday, Tuesday, and Friday lifting. Omit Thursday's hard intervals. Saturday remains Day 1.
If Tuesday is too long, reduce or omit its cardio before rushing the strength work. Shorter walks can add moderate activity elsewhere in the week.
Resume the next feasible session after a missed day. Avoid doubling heavy sessions to catch up; keep Saturday's calendar anchor.
